title: Adaptive Actor-Critic Reinforcement Learning for Differential-Drive Mobile Robots: A Sim-to-Real Framework

authors.name: Dr. Alexander J. Pereira
authors.affiliation: Robotics and Autonomous Systems Laboratory, Department of Mechanical Engineering, University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign

abstract: We propose Adaptive Actor-Critic Reinforcement Learning (A2CRL), a novel approach to training policies for differential-drive mobile robots that bridges simulation and real-world deployment. Despite achieving strong performance in simulation, prior work suffers from brittle sim-to-real transfer and long on-robot training times [1][2][3]. The proposed framework integrates domain randomization, online adaptive critic updates, and a lightweight safety supervisor to enable rapid adaptation on a physical platform. The proposed module is designed to run on an onboard Intel NUC with a modest GPU or on CPU-only modes for field deployment. Extensive experiments on a 0.65 m differential-drive robot in a 6 m by 6 m indoor arena demonstrate that our method achieves 95.4% navigation success and mean control latency 12.3 ms while reducing on-robot training wall-clock time by 62% compared to baseline PPO [4][5]. Our method maintains stable performance under battery drain and sensor noise, showing broad applicability for industrial inspection and logistics robots.

section1.title: INTRODUCTION
content: Mobile robots are increasingly deployed for logistics, inspection, and service tasks where autonomy and adaptability are essential. Reinforcement learning (RL) provides a principled framework for learning control policies from interaction without hand-designed heuristics, enabling complex navigation and decision-making behaviors in unstructured environments. However, real-world deployment of RL on resource-constrained mobile robots remains challenging due to limited onboard compute, safety concerns during exploration, and the well-known sim-to-real gap caused by mismatches in dynamics, sensors, and noise characteristics between simulators and physical platforms [1][6].

Recent advances in deep RL have produced high-performing agents in simulation using policy gradient and actor-critic algorithms such as PPO, DDPG, and SAC. Despite achieving 80–95% success in benchmark tasks, prior work suffers from long training times and sensitivity to sensor noise and actuation delays when moved to hardware [2][3][4]. Several studies advocate episodic fine-tuning on hardware or domain randomization in simulation to improve transfer, but these approaches either demand significant robot-hours or do not address online adaptation and latency constraints explicitly [5][7][8].

The central problem addressed in this paper is how to design an RL training and deployment pipeline that permits rapid sim-to-real transfer, safe online adaptation, and low-latency control on typical differential-drive platforms. We focus on a representative hardware testbed, a 0.65 m differential-drive mobile robot instrumented with Lidar, RGB-D camera, IMU, wheel encoders, and an Intel NUC-class onboard computer. The research gap is that few prior systems combine adaptive actor-critic updates, explicit safety supervision, and practical engineering design choices (sensor fusion, sampling rates, and lightweight replay buffer management) in a single, validated sim-to-real framework [3][9][10].

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews related literature on RL for robotics, sim-to-real transfer, and safety-aware learning. Section III details the system design and methodology including kinematic modeling, state estimation, actor-critic algorithm, and the safety supervisor. Section IV reports experimental results and ablation studies, including endurance testing. Section V concludes with a summary, limitations, and future work directions.

section2.title: RELATED WORK
content: This section examines the literature in three complementary threads: RL methods for control, sim-to-real transfer techniques, and safety-aware and low-latency deployment strategies. We place emphasis on works that address mobile robot navigation and real-time constraints.

section2a.title: Reinforcement Learning for Mobile Robot Control

content.text: Reinforcement learning has been applied to mobile robot navigation with varying degrees of success. Early RL navigation papers used tabular methods and function approximation for simple tasks, while modern approaches rely on deep neural network policies to map high-dimensional observations directly to control commands. Actor-critic families such as DDPG [4], PPO [5], and SAC [6] provide stable policy optimization for continuous control. DDPG introduced an off-policy deterministic policy gradient method that is sample-efficient in simulation yet often brittle on hardware due to hyperparameter sensitivity and action noise [4]. PPO introduced a clipped surrogate objective that improves stability and makes distributed training feasible [5]. SAC emphasizes entropy-regularized objectives to improve exploration and robustness to noise [6]. Despite these algorithmic advances, direct application to differential-drive mobile robots is not straightforward because of latency, odometry drift, and actuator saturation [11][12].

content.text: As shown in Fig. 1, the system architecture consists of perception, estimation, learning, and actuation modules connected by well-defined interfaces. Prior works that target mobile robot control emphasize either algorithmic novelty or system-level integration but rarely both [7][13]. Our system integrates recent actor-critic advances with practical engineering: state estimation via EKF, asynchronous prioritized replay, and a safety supervisor that enforces constraints during exploration.

Sim-to-real transfer techniques such as domain randomization, system identification, and fine-tuning on hardware have been widely studied. Domain randomization perturbs visual textures, dynamics parameters, and sensor noise in simulation to produce policies that generalize to real sensors [8][9]. System identification methods attempt to match simulator parameters to the physical system, reducing the gap but requiring precise calibration [14]. Recent work demonstrates that a combination of domain randomization in simulation plus limited online fine-tuning on hardware yields practical performance for manipulation and locomotion [10][15]. However, these methods often overlook latency and compute constraints; on-board training is rarely feasible on small robots without careful algorithmic and software design [16].

Safety during RL exploration is paramount for mobile robots operating in shared human environments. Approaches include constrained RL, shielding, and safety supervisors that can override unsafe actions [17][18]. Low-latency deployment requires attention to inference time, communication delay, and control loop frequency. Works that explicitly address real-time constraints combine model compression, control supervisor layers, and prioritized computation scheduling to meet strict deadlines [11][19]. Our design builds on these insights by employing a safety supervisor, model quantization for inference, and prioritized sampling to reduce on-robot training time while preserving safety guarantees.

section3.title: SYSTEM DESIGN AND METHODOLOGY
content: This section details the overall approach including hardware, kinematics, state estimation, algorithmic design for the actor-critic agent, and communication/integration elements. We emphasize equations describing kinematics and learning objectives and present engineering choices that enable low-latency execution.

content.text: The A2CRL system combines onboard sensing and compute with an optional external training server during pretraining. As shown in Fig. 2, the system architecture consists of sensor drivers for Lidar, RGB-D camera, IMU, and wheel encoders feeding a perception stack that performs obstacle detection and semantic segmentation at rates $f_{\mathrm{cam}}=30\ \mathrm{Hz}$ and $f_{\mathrm{lidar}}=10\ \mathrm{Hz}$. The State Estimator fuses odometry and IMU using an extended Kalman filter running at $100\ \mathrm{Hz}$ to produce $x_t$ and $\theta_t$ estimates for control. The Policy Network (actor) outputs continuous velocity commands while the Value Network (critic) supports advantage estimation for stable learning. The Control Supervisor monitors safety constraints and can override actions via a local low-latency path.

content.text: The modular design separates perception, estimation, learning, and actuation for ease of development and debugging. The proposed module is designed to run onboard an Intel NUC (model i7) with optional GPU for faster fine-tuning; however, the control loop is engineered to meet $f_{\mathrm{control}}=50\ \mathrm{Hz}$ in CPU-only mode. This constrained latencies requirement guided our selection of network size (three fully connected layers for actor and critic) and use of quantized inference kernels during deployment.

Equation (1) describes the odometry-based pose update used in our state estimator where $\Delta s_k$ is the incremental forward displacement computed from wheel encoders and $\Delta\theta_k$ is the measured rotation. Accurate updates are crucial because the RL agent conditions on the state $s_t = [x_t, y_t, \theta_t, v_t]$ where $v_t$ denotes linear velocity and sensor readings are included as observations. We found that careful calibration of encoder resolution and wheel radius reduced drift to under $0.08\ \mathrm{m}$ over 50 m trajectories.

The experimental platform is a custom differential-drive mobile robot built at the University of Illinois Robotics and Autonomous Systems Laboratory. The chassis measures $0.65\ \mathrm{m}$ length and $0.45\ \mathrm{m}$ width and carries sensors and compute described in Table I. Power is supplied by a 48 V Li-ion battery pack with on-board DC-DC converters. Motor controllers are PWM-driven H-bridge drivers controlled by the MCU and supervised by the onboard Intel NUC running Ubuntu 20.04 and ROS2 Foxy. As shown in Fig. 3, sensors are arranged to provide overlapping coverage for perception and state estimation. The proposed hardware is engineered to support low-latency inference and safe actuation.

Table I summarizes the hardware. The motor controllers provide current sensing for closed-loop torque estimation and the IMU provides 200 Hz inertial measurements. We emphasize realistic hardware constraints: limited GPU memory, thermal throttling in long experiments, and battery voltage sag under load. These considerations motivated our low-latency control design and onboard fine-tuning strategy to avoid heavy GPU dependence during deployment.

content.text: We adopt an actor-critic architecture where the actor policy $\pi_{\theta}(a|s)$ produces continuous velocity commands $a_t = [v_t, \omega_t]$ and the critic estimates state-action values for advantage calculation. Training proceeds in two stages: (i) pretraining in a high-fidelity simulator with domain randomization, and (ii) on-robot fine-tuning using prioritized experience replay with adaptive learning rates. The algorithm uses advantage estimates computed via temporal-difference returns and a value baseline to reduce variance. The online update frequency is throttled to preserve control loop stability; we interleave $N_{\mathrm{act}}=5$ control steps per training update to meet real-time constraints. The policy loss uses the policy gradient with advantage estimator while the critic minimizes TD-error.

Equation (2) defines the discounted return $G_t$ with discount factor $\gamma\in(0,1)$ which balances immediate and future rewards. In our navigation task the reward $r_t$ combines proximity to goal, collision penalties, and control smoothness terms. Specifically, $r_t = r_{\mathrm{goal}} - 5\cdot r_{\mathrm{collision}} - 0.01\|a_t\|^2$, where $r_{\mathrm{goal}}$ gives positive reinforcement upon approach.

Equation (3) is the Bellman optimality relation for the state-action value. While we do not learn Q* directly, the critic approximates $Q^{\pi}(s,a)$ to compute advantage $A(s,a)=Q^{\pi}(s,a)-V^{\pi}(s)$. Our critic is trained with TD(0) targets and bootstrapping to accelerate learning. We found that clipping TD targets and normalizing advantages stabilizes updates on hardware where sensor noise introduces variance.

The actor objective minimizes the negative expected advantage-weighted log-probability. Training uses gradient ascent on $J(\theta)$ implemented with Adam optimizer and an adaptive learning rate schedule that reduces $\alpha$ when validation success stalls. The actor update is computed every $N_{\mathrm{train}}$ steps and teacher policy actions from simulation are used to initialize weights for faster convergence.

Equation (4) shows the policy gradient objective where $A(s_t,a_t)$ is the advantage. In practice we approximate the expectation by mini-batch sampling from the replay buffer. We use prioritized replay with priority proportional to absolute TD error to focus updates on informative transitions. To limit overfitting to anomalous transitions caused by sensor faults, we cap priorities and apply importance sampling weights during gradient computation.

content.text: The communication architecture supports asynchronous data flows among perception, estimation, learning, and actuation subsystems. We use ROS2 for intra-robot messaging with DDS middleware configured for low-latency transport. High-bandwidth sensor streams are throttled and compressed before being sent to the learning module to avoid saturating the CPU. For pretraining, the simulator synchronizes with a remote training server via a 100 Mbps WiFi link; during deployment the robot operates autonomously with occasional telemetry uplinks for logging. The proposed control pipeline is designed to meet a scan-to-act latency budget $T_{\mathrm{lat}} \le 20\ \mathrm{ms}$ when running on CPU-only mode.

content.text: Equation (5) is the Kalman gain used in the EKF update step where $P_k^{-}$ is the prior covariance, $H$ is the observation matrix, and $R$ is the measurement covariance. We tune $R$ to reflect increased sensor noise under low-light or heavy payload conditions, enabling the EKF to rely more on odometry when camera data is degraded. This adaptive tuning improves state stability, which is critical because the RL policy assumes reasonably accurate state estimates at run time.

section4.title: EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS AND ANALYSIS
content: We validate A2CRL on navigation tasks in an indoor arena and perform ablations on domain randomization, prioritized replay, and safety supervision. Experiments measure navigation success, control latency, sample efficiency, and endurance under battery sag and sensor noise.

content.text: Experiments were conducted in a 6 m by 6 m indoor arena at the University of Illinois Robotics Lab. The arena contains static obstacles and movable boxes as described in Fig. 6. We instrument the arena with AprilTag fiducials and Vicon cameras to obtain ground truth for evaluation. Training uses a PyBullet-based simulator with domain randomization on mass, friction, sensor noise, and visual textures. Pretraining uses 50k simulated episodes and on-robot fine-tuning uses up to 5k episodes with early stopping based on a validation set. Key experimental parameters are summarized in Table II.

content.text: We evaluate navigation success, sample efficiency, and latency. The main metric is navigation success rate defined as reaching the goal without collision within an episode length of 1000 steps. Secondary metrics include mean control latency and average return. Table III presents results for the proposed A2CRL method averaged over 50 trials and compared against PPO and DDPG baselines. The proposed method attains $\mathrm{Accuracy}=95.4\%$ navigation success and mean latency 12.3 ms, outperforming baselines in both success and real-time performance.

Analysis of Table III shows that A2CRL reduces on-robot fine-tuning time by 62% relative to PPO baseline due to prioritized replay and adaptive learning rate scheduling. Fig. 7 visualizes training reward and validation success curves across 2000 episodes, illustrating faster convergence and lower variance. We measure control latency by timing the sensor-to-actuation pipeline including inference. The mean latency 12.3 ms meets our design goal $T_{\mathrm{lat}}\le 20\ \mathrm{ms}$ under CPU-only operation, enabling stable 50 Hz control.

content.text: Equation (6) describes gradient updates to policy parameters where $\alpha$ is the learning rate. In our implementation we adapt $\alpha$ based on plateau detection on the validation success metric and reduce it by factor 0.5 when progress stalls for 200 episodes. This adaptive schedule improved fine-tuning stability and avoided catastrophic forgetting of behaviors learned in simulation.

section4c.title: Comparison with Existing Methods / Ablation Study

content.text: We compare A2CRL with recent baselines including PPO, DDPG, and a Behavioural Cloning (BC) baseline trained on expert demonstrations. Table IV summarizes the primary quantitative comparison. Ablation studies remove domain randomization, prioritized replay, and the safety supervisor to quantify their contributions. Removing domain randomization reduced success to 81.7%, removing prioritized replay increased on-robot fine-tuning time by 85%, and disabling the safety supervisor increased collision rate by 320% under noisy sensors. These ablations demonstrate that each component contributes meaningfully to sim-to-real robustness.

content.text: As presented in Table IV, the proposed method surpasses baselines in both accuracy and latency trade-offs for CPU-only hardware. The BC baseline achieves low latency but poor generalization. PPO attains competitive accuracy in simulation but suffers higher inference latency due to a larger network and less efficient prioritization. Our method achieves Pareto-efficient performance by balancing model size and prioritized learning.

We conducted an endurance test of 48 hours continuous operation focusing on reliability under battery voltage sag and thermal conditions. The robot repeatedly executed randomized navigation episodes with periodic charging cycles removed to stress battery discharge behavior. Table V summarizes endurance test results. The system maintained navigation success above 90% until battery voltage dropped below 44 V, at which point safety supervisor engaged conservative actions and requested a recharge. Fig. 9 shows latency and battery voltage over time; mean latency remained 12.3 ms with occasional spikes to 25 ms during thermal throttling events.

section5.title: CONCLUSION
content: We propose A2CRL, a novel approach to adaptive actor-critic reinforcement learning for differential-drive mobile robots that integrates domain randomization, prioritized replay, and a safety supervisor to enable robust sim-to-real transfer. The proposed module is designed to operate within onboard latency budgets and to require minimal GPU resources. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method achieves 95.4% navigation success and mean control latency 12.3 ms while reducing on-robot fine-tuning time by 62% relative to strong baselines (Table IV, Fig. 7).

Despite achieving high success rates, the system has limitations. The current policy conditions on state estimates that, while accurate under typical conditions, degrade under extreme sensor occlusion; in such scenarios the safety supervisor can be conservative and reduce mission effectiveness. Thermal throttling under prolonged endurance tests caused occasional latency spikes, indicating a need for improved thermal management or more efficient models. The sim-to-real gains rely on realistic simulation models; poorly calibrated simulators reduce transfer effectiveness despite domain randomization.

Future work will focus on three directions: (1) integrating learned dynamics models to improve sample efficiency during on-robot fine-tuning; (2) deploying model compression and distillation techniques to further reduce inference latency for smaller embedded platforms; (3) extending safety guarantees through formal verification of the supervisor and by integrating constrained RL methods that explicitly incorporate state and action constraints. We also plan larger-scale trials in semi-structured industrial environments to validate scalability and interoperability with fleet management systems.
